passages.t: ‘Declare to the next generation’: the story told as a warning
passages.happening:
Psalm 78 is the second longest psalm, after Psalm 119. It is Israel's story told as a lesson. The heading reads, “A Maskil of Asaph” (verse 1). The teacher calls, “Give ear, O my people, to my instruction” (verse 1). “I will open my mouth in parables” (verse 2).

Then he says why. “We will not hide them from their children, but will declare to the next generation the praises of the LORD and His might, and the wonders He has performed” (verse 4). The goal is that children will trust God and keep his commands, and “Then they will not be like their fathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation” (verse 8).

The story begins. God split the sea and led them with cloud and fire (verses 13 to 14). He brought water from the rock (verses 15 to 16). But they tested God and asked, “Can God really prepare a table in the wilderness?” (verse 19). He gave them manna, ‘the bread of angels’ (verse 25), and meat as thick as dust (verse 27). Yet they kept on sinning (verse 32).

Then the turn that runs through the whole psalm: “And yet He was compassionate; He forgave their iniquity and did not destroy them” (verse 38). “He remembered that they were but flesh, a passing breeze that does not return” (verse 39).
passages.hearers:
Israel was told to teach the story to their children. Moses said that when a son asked what God's laws meant, the parent should answer, “We were slaves of Pharaoh in Egypt, but the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand” (Deuteronomy 6:21). Psalm 78 is that answer, sung.

But it is a surprising kind of family history. Most nations praise their founders. This psalm tells the children how often their ancestors failed. It names their doubt, their grumbling and their short memory. The point is not to shame the dead. It is to warn the living. Do not be like that. Remember what God has done.

The stories it uses would be well known: the manna, the quail in Numbers 11, the water from the rock in Exodus 17. A hearer would fill in the details. The psalm moves fast and trusts the listener to know them.
passages.later:
Matthew quotes verse 2 when he tells of Jesus teaching in parables: “I will open My mouth in parables; I will utter things hidden since the foundation of the world” (Matthew 13:35).

Jesus spoke of the manna: “it was not Moses who gave you the bread from heaven, but it is My Father who gives you the true bread from heaven” (John 6:32). And Paul, telling the same wilderness story to the church in Corinth, said, “Now these things happened to them as examples and were written down as warnings for us” (1 Corinthians 10:11).
passages.asks:
Who is the next generation in your life? A child, a grandchild, a young person at church, a neighbour's teenager. Psalm 78 says the story of God is not passed on by accident. Someone has to tell it.

And tell it honestly. The psalm does not hide the failures. Faith that is handed on with the failures left in may last longer than faith handed on as a polished tale. If no one passed the story to you, it is not too late to learn it, and to become the one who tells it.

passages.t: From Egypt to Shiloh to David: ‘He chose David His servant’
passages.happening:
The teacher goes back over the story a second time. “How often they disobeyed Him in the wilderness and grieved Him in the desert” (verse 40). They forgot the plagues God sent on Egypt (verses 43 to 51). God led them out like sheep and brought them to his holy land (verses 52 to 55).

But in the land they did the same again. They “were faithless like their fathers, twisted like a faulty bow” (verse 57). They worshipped idols on the hilltops (verse 58). So God “abandoned the tabernacle of Shiloh” (verse 60) and let his people fall to their enemies (verses 61 to 64).

Then, suddenly, God acts. “Then the Lord awoke as from sleep, like a mighty warrior overcome by wine” (verse 65). He chose Judah and Mount Zion (verse 68). “He chose David His servant and took him from the sheepfolds” (verse 70). The psalm ends with a shepherd king: “So David shepherded them with integrity of heart and guided them with skillful hands” (verse 72).
passages.hearers:
Shiloh was where the tent of meeting stood before there was a temple. In the days of Samuel the ark of God was carried from Shiloh into battle and lost: “The ark of God was captured” (1 Samuel 4:11). Verses 60 to 64 grieve that day. Jeremiah later pointed to Shiloh as a warning to Jerusalem (Jeremiah 7:12).

Verse 65 is a bold picture. God does not really sleep: “the Protector of Israel will neither slumber nor sleep” (Psalm 121:4). The psalm is telling how it looked from Israel's side. For years God seemed to do nothing. Then he roused himself like a warrior.

‘Ephraim’ and ‘Joseph’ (verses 9 and 67) were the leading northern tribes. The psalm sets their failure beside God's choice of Judah, David's tribe. Scholars date the psalm differently, some to David's or Solomon's day and some to after the north fell to Assyria. The psalm itself does not say.
passages.later:
The shepherd king of verse 70 points ahead. Jesus said, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep” (John 10:11). David was taken from the sheepfolds to lead God's people. Jesus, the Son of David, gave his life for them.

Paul tells the same story of rebellion and mercy in Romans 9 to 11, and ends in praise of God's mercy.
passages.asks:
Psalm 78 tells the story twice, and both times God's people fail. Both times God is still there at the end. That is the hope of the psalm. Not that the people got better, but that God did not give up.

Read the story of your own life the same way. Where have you forgotten what God did? And where, after all of it, has he still been leading you? Thank him for the shepherd he gave.
